examples: It was the biggest comeback in team history.

Their comebacks are why people watch.

senses.head: A recovery from being far behind, or a return after time away
examples: It was the biggest comeback in team history.
He's attempting a comeback at thirty-eight.
Their comebacks are why people watch.

senses.head: A quick, clever reply to a remark or an insult
examples: I thought of a great comeback about an hour too late.

He is never short of a comeback.

entries.meaning: A surprise win by the side nobody expected to win. ---
examples: The tournament's biggest upset came on day one.
There were three upsets in the first round.
Nobody called that game an upset afterward.
entries.contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, UP-set; the verb is up-SET.

entries.meaning: A second match between the same two opponents. ---
examples: The rematch is set for December.
Both rematches sold out in an hour.
He wants a rematch on his home court.

entries.meaning: Knockout has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He won by knockout in the third round.
Twenty of her wins were knockouts.
That punch was a clean knockout.
She looked like a knockout in that dress.
Their new singer is an absolute knockout.
Everyone told him his date was a knockout.

senses.head: A win in boxing when the other fighter cannot get back up
examples: He won by knockout in the third round.
Twenty of her wins were knockouts.
That punch was a clean knockout.

senses.head: An extremely attractive person
examples: She looked like a knockout in that dress.
Their new singer is an absolute knockout.
Everyone told him his date was a knockout.

entries.meaning: A pairing of two teams or players against each other. ---
examples: It's a tough matchup for a young defense.
The matchups were announced this morning.
That matchup has been building for years.

entries.meaning: The long-running competition between two teams or players. ---
examples: The rivalry goes back to 1902.
College football has the fiercest rivalries.
Their rivalry sells out every stadium.

entries.meaning: The illegal use of drugs to improve athletic performance. ---
examples: Two runners were banned for doping.
Doping controls are done after every race.
The doping scandal cost the country its medals.

entries.meaning: The act of putting a fresh player in for one already on the field. ---
examples: The coach made his last substitution in the eightieth minute.
Teams get five substitutions now.
That substitution changed the game.
entries.contrast: Americans say sub-stih-TOO-shuhn; the British add a y sound: -TYOO-.

entries.meaning: Fair, generous behavior toward opponents in a game. ---
examples: Shaking hands afterward is basic sportsmanship.
The league gives an award for sportsmanship.
His sportsmanship impressed everyone in the gym.

entries.meaning: The stretch of games played after the regular season ends. ---
examples: They haven't made the postseason since 2015.
He hit better in the postseason than in the summer.
Two straight postseasons ended in the first round.

entries.meaning: A recording of a play shown again, often to check a call.
examples: The replay showed his foot on the line.
They watched three replays before reversing the call.
Instant replay has changed how games are officiated.
entries.contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, REE-play; the verb is ree-PLAY.
